appearance.organs.leaf.shape.leaf.why: A sprig card is a leafy twig, so its leaves are the species' own size: as long as floras measure the blade and a quarter again for its stalk, on a card as long as the twig. Larger leaves, fewer of them, make a crown of a few giant leaves with sky between them.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.twigs.why: Leaves smaller than the card's longest stand on side twigs as well as the main one, as a shoot's leaves stand on its side shoots, so the twig covers about as much of its card with leaves as the area the program shades with: about two and a half side twigs for each time its leaves go into the longest a card's leaf may be (0.45 of the card), less one.

generator.params.short_share.why: Where a taxon grows short shoots, they fill most of its crown and bear most of its leaves (Wilson's red maple, Hallé, Oldeman and Tomlinson 1978, pp. 59-60): every bud of a growth unit that does not grow a long shoot grows a short one, from the nodes behind them, so each year's growth ends in long shoots with tufts of leaves behind, in a shrub as in a tree (decurrent_tree). Until 2026-10-17 a shrub grew only as many short shoots as long ones, which left beaked hazel with a quarter of a tree's leaf area per crown area. Elsewhere a third as many as the long ones, as at the seed plants.

generator.params.bud_years.why: A short shoot lives far longer than its leaves but far less than the wood, perhaps 20 years at most (Hallé, Oldeman and Tomlinson 1978, p. 60), and many die younger: almond spurs at 5 to 27 percent a year (Lampinen et al. 2011). So leaves crowd the last ten years' wood behind each tip, and older wood is bare.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.pedice.why: A cluster's flower stands on a stalk as long, for the length of the cluster and its peduncle, as floras measure them.

appearance.organs.flower.inflorescence.why: A flower borne in a cluster of known length is drawn as the cluster, its units laid out by the cluster rules; a solitary flower stays one flower, and so does one whose cluster's length no source gives.

appearance.organs.bloom.inflorescence.why: A tree's or shrub's flowers borne in clusters of known length are drawn as the clusters; solitary flowers stay single.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.unit.why: A cluster's flower is as wide, for the length of the cluster and its peduncle, as floras measure them, whichever axis bears it: a panicle's or compound umbel's flowers sit on its branches.

generator.params.flower_size.why: A herb's flowering organ is as long as its inflorescence and the peduncle it stands on where its flowers are in clusters, else as wide as its flower; where its sepals outreach its petals, the flower's width is theirs, and its petals reach that share of it.

generator.params.bloom_size.why: A tree's or shrub's bloom is as long as its inflorescence and the peduncle it stands on where its flowers are in clusters, else as wide as its flower; where its sepals outreach its petals, the flower's width is theirs, and its petals reach that share of it.

generator.params.units.why: A stem that grows on past its flowers is drawn as a sympodium: six units above the first inflorescence where one bud grows on each time, four where two do (sixteen tips), so either reaches its height in units as long as its leaves allow; one that grows on from its tip ends in a raceme.

generator.params.forks.why: One shoot grows on past each inflorescence of a monochasium, two of a dichasium.

generator.params.fork_angle.why: A monochasium's shoot grows on nearly in line, the inflorescence pushed aside, so the stem zigzags a little; a dichasium's two shoots spread apart round the flower in their fork.

generator.params.unit_leaves.why: Each unit of a sympodium bears as many leaves as its taxa state.

generator.params.geminate.why: Geminate leaves are drawn as a pair at one node, the smaller half as long as the larger.

generator.params.flower_tilt.why: A flower on a sympodium's peduncle faces as its posture says: up, at a slant, level, down and out, or straight down.

generator.params.bloom_angle.why: A woody plant's bloom stands from its shoot as the flower's posture says; past a right angle it hangs.

appearance.organs.flower.form.flower.cur.why: A flower's petals or tepals bend back from their cup as far as its flora says: not at all, a little where they spread, a quarter turn where their tips curve back (recurved), half a turn where they sweep back to the stalk (reflexed, a Turk's cap), and further where they roll (revolute).

They bend back from as far along their length as the flora says ('reflexed 2/5 along length from base'); where it gives no share, a recurved tip from three fifths, a reflexed one from about a third, a revolute one from a fifth, as the North American lilies mostly are.

appearance.organs.*.shape.spots.why: Dark spots on the inner face of each petal or tepal, toward its base: a few, many, or crowded as its flora words them (12 is as many as a flower's part keeps at full detail).

appearance.organs.*.shape.anther_colour.why: Anthers are drawn in the colour their flora gives them, apart from the look's accent.

appearance.organs.*.shape.base_colour.why: Where a flora colours the petals' or tepals' base apart from their tips, their inner face is drawn in that colour from the foot, fading into the petal's colour where it stops.

appearance.organs.*.shape.base_length.why: The base colour reaches as far along each petal or tepal as its flora says ('red-orange on distal 1/5-1/4' leaves the base colour about four fifths).

appearance.organs.*.shape.star_colour.why: Nectaries a flora says show at the foot of each petal or tepal are drawn there in their colour, together a star at the flower's heart.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stripe_colour.why: A stripe a flora names down the middle of each petal or tepal is drawn in its colour along the midrib of the inner face, from the foot.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stripe_length.why: The stripe reaches as far along each petal or tepal as its flora says; a 'proximal' stripe with no share given reaches half way, the proximal half.

appearance.organs.*.shape.back_colour.why: Where a flora colours the petals' or tepals' outer (abaxial) face apart from the inner, the outer face is drawn in that colour, as seen from behind or under a nodding flower.

appearance.organs.*.shape.back_base_colo.why: Where a flora colours the outer face's base apart from the rest, it is drawn in that colour from the foot, fading into the outer face's colour where it stops.

appearance.organs.*.shape.back_base_leng.why: The outer base colour reaches as far along each petal or tepal as its flora says ('green abaxially on proximal 2/5-1/2').

generator.params.bloom_stalk.why: A tree's or shrub's solitary flower hangs or stands on its own stalk, as long as its flora measures it, its pedicel or, where it calls a lone flower's or head's stalk a peduncle, that; a cluster's flowers keep their stalks in the cluster.

generator.params.suckers.why: A many-stemmed shrub sends up stems from its base, a few or many beside the first, and a thicket sends them up from its spreading roots, rhizomes or layered branches, more of them as they spread, in place of one stem that forks above the ground.

generator.params.sucker_spread.why: A clump's stems rise close round its crown at the ground, a few or many within a fifth of the crown's radius; a thicket's come up from roots and rhizomes running out under most of it.

generator.params.stem_life.why: A clump's or thicket's stems that floras say live only a few years (biennial canes) die back whole at the longest age they give, a thimbleberry's most at two and some at three (FEIS, Gucker 2012), so the clump never holds a stem older than that.

generator.params.sucker_rate.why: Where its stems die young the base goes on sending up new ones every year, as many a year as keep the clump at its stems: their number shared over the years each lives.

generator.params.fork_height.why: A single-stemmed woody plant stands on one trunk that never divides into equal stems; one whose flora says how high its young stem first divides forks there into its main stems.

generator.params.fork_clear.why: A woody plant whose flora says how high its young stem first divides grows that stem single up to the fork, with no limb below it.

generator.params.bloom_floor.why: A woody plant that flowers only on its growth above its first fork has no bloom below the highest its fork stands.

generator.params.bloom_hang.why: A hanging flower on its own stalk turns most of the way from its stalk toward straight down, whichever way its shoot points; floras' pendent flowers hang from straight down to nearly level.

generator.params.scape.why: A flowering stem without leaves is drawn as a leafless scape above the leaves at its foot: a thrift's or a sundew's, as a lily's.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.branch.why: A compound inflorescence's branches are laid out as the cluster its taxon names them: a pigweed's or an amaranth's panicle of dense spikes, not of racemes.

generator.params.lie.why: A decumbent stem lies on the ground for its lower half and rises over the rest; a prostrate or trailing stem lies along the ground for most of its length, only its last quarter, which bears the flowers, raised.

generator.params.lie_branch.why: A lying stem that floras call freely branching puts out a branch at about every third of its lying nodes, each lying and rising as the stem does, so the plant spreads into a mat; one they do not call so lies unbranched.

generator.params.axil_racemes.why: Where a flora says a plant's inflorescences crowd its upper leaf axils (hemp's congested pseudospikes), each leaf node of a flowering branch bears one in its axil.

generator.params.branch_nodes.why: A branch crowded with inflorescences bears them in five leaf axils below its own, as hemp's branch tips do, not the herb program's two.

generator.params.alternate_above.why: Where a flora says a stem's leaves turn alternate toward its top over pairs or whorls below (hemp's, opposite proximally and alternate distally), its upper two fifths of leafy nodes bear one leaf each.

appearance.organs.flower.colour.why: An open flower is drawn in the colour its showiest part is stated in.

appearance.organs.bloom.colour.why: A tree's or shrub's blooms are drawn in the colour its flowers' showiest part is stated in.

appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.out.why: A deciduous woody plant's leaves unfold a third of the way into the first month floras say they do, or into April, when most temperate broadleaves leaf out, where they give none. A drought-deciduous one is drawn leafless outside the one leafy season a year that floras give months for, its leaves coming with the rains (leaf_out_months) and falling as the soil dries (leaf_fall_months); where they give no months it is drawn in leaf all year, and where they give only the months it leafs out in, it holds its leaves to the year's end.

appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.full.why: Its leaves reach their full size about a month after they unfold.

appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.turn.why: Its leaves begin to turn ten days before the first month floras say they fall in, or before October where they give none.

appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.fall.why: The last of its leaves are down ten days before the last month floras say they fall in ends, or November where they give none. Months that fall before the months they unfold in are the next year's, as a southern beech's are.

appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.autumn.why: Its leaves turn the colour floras give them in autumn, or a dull yellow browning where they give none.

appearance.organs.fruit.colour.why: A fruit is drawn in the colour it is stated to ripen to; its unripe share keeps the look's accent.

appearance.organs.*.shape.aspect.why: A fruit is as wide for its length as its flora measures it; where it gives no width, as its outline's word makes it: as wide as long where globose, about twice as wide as tall where hemispheric, and narrower where ellipsoid, ovoid, obovoid, conic, cylindric, obconic or club-shaped.

appearance.organs.*.shape.flare.why: A fruit is as much wider toward its tip than its base as its outline is stated: even where round or ellipsoid, widest below its middle where ovoid, above it where obovoid, and drawn to a narrow base where obconic or club-shaped.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stigma.why: A flower's stigma lobes are drawn in the colour they are stated in, where it differs from the style's.

appearance.organs.fruit.accent.why: A fruit's unripe share, and its stalk, are drawn in the colour floras give the unripe fruit, else in the green of the plant's leaves until a colour of its own is stated.

appearance.organs.fruit.shape.seeds.why: A ripe fruit that opens on its seeds shows them in the colour they ripen to: a magnolia's red seeds hang from its split follicles.

appearance.organs.fruit.shape.ripening.why: A fruit that passes through a colour of its own as it ripens is drawn in it while most of its fruit are still unripe, then turns to its ripe colour.

appearance.organs.fruit.shape.threads.why: A ripe seed hangs below its split follicle on a thread as long, for the fruit's length, as floras measure it.

appearance.organs.fruit.shape.cup.why: A fruit that stands in a cup on a swollen stalk is drawn in one, in the colour the cup ripens to.

appearance.organs.fruit.inflorescence.fr.why: A cluster ripens as many fruit as floras count on one infructescence; its other flowers fall and leave their pedicels bare.

appearance.organs.fruit.inflorescence.un.why: A cluster's fruit is as long, for the length of the cluster and its peduncle, as floras measure them, whichever axis bears it.

appearance.organs.*.season.flower_look.s.why: A flower is as wide, for its fruit's length, as floras measure the flower and the fruit (the flower by its petals' reach where sepals outreach them, as the bloom size rule grows it): a cluster's flower against its fruit, a lone flower against the fruit it becomes.

appearance.organs.*.season.fruit_size.why: A lone flower's organ is grown as wide as its petals reach (its flower's width less sepals that outreach them, as the bloom size rule grows it), so its fruit is drawn at the fruit's stated length; a cluster grown as long as its inflorescence grows in fruit where its fruit outgrow it, to hold them on their stalks (a third again their length, as an umbel's rays need).

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.kind.why: Each kind of inflorescence is laid out as the cluster of its name, and a spadix as a spike; a solitary flower is no cluster.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.flower.why: A cluster bears the inflorescence's units, up to the 200 an axis can hold; a compound one (a compound umbel, a panicle, a compound corymb) shares them among its primary branches, so it needs their count.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.branch.why: A compound cluster bears the inflorescence's primary branches, up to 60.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.dome.why: A flat-topped corymb's flowers stand level; a rounded one's lie on a half sphere, a globose one's round a ball.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.droop.why: An erect inflorescence's axis stays straight; a nodding one bends over by a quarter turn toward its tip, a pendent one by half a turn, so it hangs.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pattern.why: A compound leaf sets its leaflets along a rachis or from the petiole's tip, as its division pattern says.

appearance.organs.*.shape.interjected.why: An interruptedly pinnate leaf bears a small pair between each two of its pairs, and between its top pair and its end leaflet, each a quarter as long as the shorter pair beside it.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pinnules.why: Each pinna of a twice-divided leaf (or each division of a biternate one) bears the leaflets floras count on it, and each of a thrice-divided one its pinnules, odd or even as the division ends, set as its divisions after the first are; a leaf divided four times or more is drawn divided three times, and one whose pinnules floras do not count, twice. A leaf divided once bears none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.segments.why: Each pinnule of a thrice-divided leaf bears the leaflets or segments floras count on it, odd or even as it ends, where floras count its pinnules too. A leaf divided once or twice has none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.inner.why: A compound leaf whose later divisions are set otherwise than its first (a ternate-pinnate leaf) draws them as its inner division pattern says.

appearance.organs.*.shape.blade_width.why: A pinnate leaf's laterals reach no farther than the blade's edge, its width over its length as floras measure them: a strap-shaped leaf's pinnae are short for their spacing.

appearance.organs.*.shape.lace.why: A divided leaf whose taxa say how its divisions are held is drawn up close as geometry, its rachises and each leaflet or segment where it stands, on the two nearest levels; farther off, on its card.

appearance.organs.*.shape.lift.why: A spray's primary divisions rise a quarter of a right angle out of the leaf's plane; a flat leaf's and a bottlebrush's do not.

appearance.organs.*.shape.scatter.why: Each division turns a little at random about its rachis: hardly in a flat leaf, up to 30 degrees either way in a spray, 20 round a bottlebrush.

appearance.organs.*.shape.roll.why: A bottlebrush's primary divisions turn round the rachis by the golden angle from one to the next, so they stand all round it; a flat leaf's and a spray's keep two ranks.

appearance.organs.*.shape.inner_roll.why: A bottlebrush's leaflets or segments turn round their division's rachis by the golden angle too; a flat leaf's and a spray's lie in their division's plane.

appearance.organs.*.shape.confluent.why: A blade dissected into fine segments is drawn as a divided leaf whose segments run together along a winged rachis; a compound leaf's leaflets stand apart.

appearance.organs.*.shape.perianth.why: A calyx and corolla draws one whorl of petals with sepals below them; like tepals draw two whorls; a spiral, tepals on a spiral; no perianth, none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_ratio.why: A petal is as wide for its length as its outline is stated: a narrow strap (linear) to as broad as long (orbicular) or a fan as broad as long (flabellate), drawn among as many petals as the flower has. Where every flower is sterile, the petals drawn are its showy sepals, as their outline is stated (sterile_sepal_shape).

appearance.organs.*.shape.taper.why: A petal narrows from its widest to its tip as its outline is stated: straight sides to a point (lanceolate, ovate), a curve (elliptic), or round and full to the tip (obovate, spatulate, orbicular, oblong), a fan squarest of all (flabellate). Where every flower is sterile, the petals drawn are its showy sepals, as their outline is stated (sterile_sepal_shape).

appearance.organs.*.shape.point.why: A petal's tip is as pointed as stated: drawn out (acuminate), pointed (acute), blunt (obtuse), or round (rounded, truncate, and a notched tip's lobes).

appearance.organs.*.shape.notch.why: An emarginate petal's tip is notched; a bilobed one is cleft into two lobes.

tepals.rule: first(perianth_parts, 0) > 0 ? clamp(max(round(perianth_parts / clamp(round(flower_merosity), 2, 6)), 1), 1, 6) * clamp(round(flower_merosity), 2, 6) : clamp(2 * round(flower_merosity), 4, 12)

appearance.organs.*.shape.petals.why: A flower draws its merosity's petals in each whorl its corolla is stated to stand in, never fewer than three (a poppy's 2 + 2 draws four, a lone whorl of two draws three); twice it in tepals, or the stated tepals rounded to whole whorls of its merosity (an amaranth's 5 as one whorl, a magnolia's 12 as four whorls of three); or a spiral's tepals in all, up to 160 (an ice plant's 100 to 150 petal-like staminodes).

appearance.organs.*.shape.sepals.why: A calyx has as many sepals as the flower's merosity; tepals and a spiral's outer tepals are drawn as the perianth itself. A cluster whose flowers are all sterile (a mophead hydrangea's) draws no calyx below them: their showy petaloid sepals are its corolla, in the flower's colour.

appearance.organs.*.shape.corolla.why: A zygomorphic flower's parts differ by place as its zygomorphy says, and one of no named kind draws its upper petal unlike the rest, wider and more upright; a regular flower, even in a family whose zygomorphic flowers are of a kind, is drawn with its petals alike.

appearance.organs.*.shape.fused.why: A bell, funnel, tube or urn is a corolla whose petals are joined for that share of their length; a flat or cupped one has them free.

appearance.organs.*.shape.throat.why: A tube's mouth, over a petal's length: wide for a bell, narrow for a tube, narrower for a salver's or an urn's.

appearance.organs.*.shape.tube_reach.why: A corolla tube a flora measures is drawn that long, over the flower's radius, however short its lobes leave it: a trumpet longer than it is wide.

appearance.organs.*.shape.tube_colour.why: A joined corolla's tube is drawn in its own colour where it is stated apart from the lobes'.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_rise.why: Petals or corolla lobes stand up, out nearly flat, or bent back toward the stalk as their posture says: reflexed ones sharply back, nearly along it, as a shooting star's are swept back from its beak of anthers.

appearance.organs.*.shape.sepal_rise.why: Sepals stand up against the corolla, out flat, or bent back toward the stalk as their posture says.

appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx.why: Sepals, and a floral tube that bears them, are drawn in their stated colour; where none is stated, floras' green sepals are the plant's own green (an opium poppy's glaucous blue-green bud), and leaf green where no leaf colour is stated either.

appearance.organs.*.shape.nod.why: A cluster's flower faces along its pedicel; a nodding one turns most of the way down from where it is borne, and a pendent one hangs straight down (a bleeding heart's hearts).

appearance.organs.*.shape.disc.why: A capsule crowned by its stigmatic disc bears it as a low dome with a ray for each carpel, as many as floras count (a poppy's 5 to 18).

appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_shed.why: A caducous calyx falls as the flower opens (a poppy's two sepals, pushed off as a cap), so a bud wears it and an open flower shows none; any other calyx stays.

appearance.organs.*.shape.sepal_length.why: A sepal is as long, for a petal's length, as its flora measures both; where it measures no petal, for the flower's radius, as a joined corolla's limb reaches.

appearance.organs.*.shape.sepals_fused.why: A calyx is joined into a tube for all its length but its free lobes or teeth, as floras measure the calyx and its lobes.

appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_angled.why: An angled calyx tube is drawn with a ridge down each sepal's midrib and a groove between them; a terete one round.

appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_swell.why: A calyx tube swollen at its base bulges out low down, most a third of the way up, by about a third of its mouth's width; an even one does not.

appearance.organs.*.shape.floral_tube.why: A floral tube a flora measures above an inferior ovary is drawn that long, over the radius its petals reach. A sterile flower is all spread calyx, with no tube below it.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stamen_length.why: Stamens reach as far, for a petal's length, as their flora says: within the perianth, just to its mouth, well out of it, or past its tips. Where it gives no such words, a stamen it measures is drawn that long, over the radius the petals reach, so long-exserted stamens hang out past them, and a magnolia's 2 to 3 cm in a flower 20 cm across reaches a fifth of the way out. A stamen it measures beside a petal it measures is drawn in their ratio whatever words it uses, so a fairy duster's 2 cm stamens stand four times its 5 mm petals out of the flower.

appearance.organs.*.shape.style_length.why: A style a flora measures apart from the stamens is drawn that long, over the radius the petals reach.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stamen_lean.why: Connivent anthers lean together in a cone round the style; free ones spread a little.

appearance.organs.*.shape.belly.why: An urn swells in its middle and narrows to its mouth.

appearance.organs.*.shape.tube.why: A hypanthium is a floral cup under the perianth, 0.4 of the flower's radius long. A sterile flower is all spread calyx, with no floral cup below it.

appearance.organs.*.shape.ovary.why: The ovary sits inside the whorls, half below them, or below them.

appearance.organs.*.shape.turn.why: A resupinate flower is drawn turned half round, so a lip formed toward the axis hangs below.

appearance.organs.*.shape.anther_tilt.why: An anther stands along its filament where the filament joins its base, leans where it joins its back, and lies nearly across the filament's tip where it swings free (versatile), as Simpson defines the three.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stamens.why: A flower draws its stamens, up to 400. A sterile flower (a mophead hydrangea's) draws none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.staminodes.why: A flower draws its sterile stamens without anthers, up to 50. A sterile flower (a mophead hydrangea's) draws none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.carpels.why: A flower draws one pistil of up to five carpels, or of any number in an inferior ovary; above five in a superior one, as many free pistils, up to 100. A sterile flower (a mophead hydrangea's) draws none.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_whorls.why: A corolla stands in the whorls it is stated in.

appearance.organs.*.shape.whorl.why: Tepals whose number is stated stand in whorls of the flower's merosity (an amaranth's one whorl of five, a magnolia's three, four or five whorls of three); otherwise in two whorls of half each.

appearance.organs.*.shape.stamen_width.why: A filament is a slender thread; a laminar stamen is a flat strap about a sixth as wide as it is long.

appearance.organs.*.shape.anther.why: A laminar stamen bears its pollen sacs along most of its length, over a short foot.

appearance.organs.*.shape.filament.why: A flower's filaments and styles are drawn in the colour its filaments are stated in; its anthers keep the accent.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pistil.why: A flower's ovaries and its free carpels are drawn in the colour its carpels are stated in at flowering.

appearance.organs.*.shape.torus.why: Free carpels on an elongate receptacle stand on a spiral up a cone as long, over the flower's radius, as the gynoecium is stated (a third of the radius where it is not), the stamens crowded round its foot; on a flat or convex one, round a low dome.

appearance.organs.flower.accent.why: A spotted flower's spots are drawn in their stated colour, the look's accent (its anthers then in their own, `anther_colour`); an unspotted flower's anthers, and its centre where it draws no stamens, in the colour its anthers are stated in.

appearance.organs.bloom.accent.why: A tree's or shrub's blooms draw their anthers, and their centre where they draw no stamens, in the colour its anthers are stated in.

appearance.organs.*.shape.bud.why: A lone flower's closed bud shows the colour its bud is stated in: its sepals', or the bracts' that wrap it.

appearance.organs.*.shape.rise.why: A rotate corolla's petals spread nearly flat, 10 degrees above the plane square to the axis; a cupped one's rise 55 degrees into a bowl; other forms keep the drawn default of 30.

generator.params.bud_size.why: A herb's largest bud is as long as floras measure a bud about to open.

generator.params.nod.why: A nodding bud hangs nearly upside down from its stalk; an erect one stands straight.

generator.params.hook.why: A nodding bud's stalk bends over only in its top part, hooked just below the bud, and stands straight below that.

generator.params.fruit_length.why: A herb's fruit is as long as floras measure it at its longest.

generator.params.fruit_size.why: A fruit is as long as floras measure it at its longest.

appearance.organs.*.shape.fruitlets.why: An aggregate fruit is drawn with as many drupelets as floras count, each as large as that many need to cover it: a cloudberry's few large ones, a raspberry's many small ones.

appearance.organs.*.shape.loose.why: An aggregate's drupelets hold together as floras say: packed into one firm fruit where strongly coherent, each a separate bead round a small core where weakly coherent.

appearance.organs.*.shape.hairs.why: A hairy fruit's fine pale hairs dull and pale its colour, the more the denser they are: a little where puberulent, most where tomentose.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_calyx.why: A calyx that stays on the fruit is drawn under it, its lobes as long, for the fruit's width, as floras measure the calyx in fruit; where they do not, a third of the fruit's width and clasping its foot, and one that grows on after flowering spreading in a star nearly as long as the fruit is wide; one that breaks off round its base leaves a rim a fifth of the fruit's width under it.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_prickles.why: A prickly calyx kept as a cap on the fruit bears its prickles there, as long as floras measure them.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_posture.why: A kept calyx lies as floras say it does: a clasping one is pressed over the fruit's base as a cap, its lobes following the fruit up from the stalk; a spreading one stands out flat in a star; a reflexed one turns back toward the stalk. Where no posture is stated, short lobes rise a little round the fruit's foot and long ones spread.

appearance.organs.fruit.shape.seed_size.why: An opened capsule's seeds are as long, for the fruit's length, as floras measure the seed and the fruit.

appearance.organs.*.shape.valves.why: A ripe capsule splits from its tip into as many valves as floras count, each turned out from about half way down; an unripe one stays shut.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_lobes.why: A kept calyx has as many lobes as the flower's merosity; the rim a calyx leaves where it broke off round its base is torn into twice as many.

appearance.organs.*.shape.hang.why: A fruit is held as floras say it is: a pendent one hangs straight down from where it is borne, a deflexed one turns half way down, an erect one stands nearly upright, a spreading one keeps its stalk's line.

appearance.organs.*.shape.armed.why: A prickly fruit is drawn with stout prickles all over, a bristly one with fine bristles, a hooked one with fine bristles bent back at their tips.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kind.why: A fruit whose flora says what its free pistils make is drawn as that: drupelets, follicles on a cone-like axis, samaras up a spindle, separate berries from one stalk, achenes in a hip, or achenes on a fleshy receptacle (a strawberry). Otherwise a berry or drupe is drawn as an ellipsoid, and so is a dry one-seeded fruit (an achene, cypsela, grain or nut) in its own dull colour; a pome dimpled at its top; a capsule, follicle or schizocarp ribbed lengthwise; a legume or other pod long, flat and bulging over its seeds; a samara as a seed at the base of a wing; an aggregate or multiple fruit as a cluster of drupelets. A nut's cup or husk and a berry's crown are the lineage's to say.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.pedunc.why: A cluster stands on a bare stalk, its peduncle, its share of the stalk and the cluster together; a cluster's units or branches begin above it. Where no peduncle is stated the organ is the cluster alone, as long as floras measure it from its lowest unit or branch, so its units begin at its foot.

appearance.organs.*.shape.spur.why: A spur is drawn as long as its length over the flower's radius, up to three radii.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.template.why: A leaf of separate leaflets is drawn on a compound card, whose pattern the leaf rules set; a blade cut from one point on a palmate card, one cut along its midrib on a lobed card, and an uncut one on a simple card.

generator.params.thorns.why: An armed tree or shrub carries its prickles or thorns at the nodes, beside each bud: a rose's below its stipules, a bramble's on its canes, a hawthorn's thorns in the leaf axils; one whose thorns only tip its twigs bears none there; programs that grow no thorns leave it unread.

generator.params.thorn_length.why: A prickle or thorn is drawn as long as its flora measures it.

generator.params.thorn_angle.why: A prickle or thorn leaves its shoot at the angle its flora gives: leaning toward the shoot's tip where ascending, square to it where erect, back toward its base where declined (retrorse). A prickle whose flora does not say stands square to its stem, as most do.

generator.params.thorn_pair.why: A thorn that is a shoot, or a leafless thorn in an axil, stands alone beside its bud (a hawthorn's, a citrus's); stipular spines stand in a pair at the node, one in each stipule's place (a black locust's).

generator.params.thorn_share.why: A shoot bears its thorns on as many of its nodes as its flora says: few, about one node in five; numerous, three in five; or every node (by eye from photographs of hawthorns and locusts; imagekit counts can set them).

generator.params.thorn_spread.why: A plant's thorns or prickles run from the shortest to the longest its flora measures, about its middle length (a hawthorn's 7 mm terminal thorns to its 24 mm lateral ones).

generator.params.thorn_years.why: A thorn or prickle stays on its stem as long as its flora says: two years where only the young stems are armed (the stem hairs' youth), five where they persist a few years (a hawthorn's), for good where they persist.

generator.params.thorn_tips.why: A shoot whose twigs end in thorns ends about half its long shoots' years in one where they are terminal, a quarter where its thorns are both terminal and lateral (by eye from photographs of palo verdes and hawthorns; imagekit counts can set them).

appearance.organs.thorn.form.why: A thorn, a shoot turned spine (a hawthorn's, a mesquite's), is drawn as a straight slender cone standing from the stem's surface beside its bud.

appearance.organs.thorn.form.prickles.be.why: A prickle grows from the stem's skin (a rose's, a bramble's, a devil's club's), so it is drawn as a flattened cone on the stem's surface at each node and, as thickly as its flora says, between the nodes: on a stem 1 cm across about one every 7 cm where sparse, one every 2 cm where moderate, about four a centimetre where dense (sparse and moderate by eye from photographs of roses and brambles; dense counted on devil's club's older stems, about 430 a metre at 1 cm, imagekit run devils-club-prickles-by-eye-2026-10-19, the young tips bearing three times that), and more on a stouter stem, as a flora's density is of the stem's skin.

appearance.organs.thorn.form.prickles.br.why: Needle-like aciculi and bristles among the prickles are drawn as thin needles a third a prickle's length: on a stem 1 cm across about one every 2.5 cm where sparse, one every 3 mm where they cover it (a beach rose's young canes).

appearance.organs.thorn.form.prickles.be.why: A stem whose prickles are scattered between its nodes, as a catclaw's are, bears none at the nodes themselves.

appearance.organs.thorn.shape.template.why: A thorn or prickle is drawn from a blade card: its length the organ's, its foot's width the card's aspect, narrowing to a point.

appearance.organs.thorn.shape.aspect.why: A thorn's or prickle's foot is as wide for its length as its flora measures it; where it gives no width, a thorn's about an eighth of its length (a slender cone, as the legumes' thorns are drawn) and a prickle's two fifths (a flora's ordinary broad-based prickle; subulate ones are narrower, deltoid ones as wide as long).

appearance.organs.thorn.shape.taper.why: A thorn or prickle narrows from its foot to a sharp tip.

appearance.organs.thorn.bend.droop.why: A prickle bends back toward the stem's base from foot to tip as its flora says: not at all where straight (erect, subulate), about a third of a right angle where curved, nearly a right angle where hooked, as a blackberry's and a dog rose's are.

appearance.organs.thorn.colour.why: A thorn or prickle is drawn in the colour its flora gives it, or else in its bark's: the young stem's skin it grows from.

appearance.organs.basal.shape.template.why: A rosette's leaves are the species' leaves, unless their own are stated. A leaf of separate leaflets is drawn on a compound card, whose pattern the leaf rules set; a blade cut from one point on a palmate card, one cut along its midrib on a lobed card, and an uncut one on a simple card.

appearance.organs.bloom.shape.template.why: Single flowers are drawn on a flower card, heads of florets on a head card and spikelets on a spikelet card; the inflorescence rules lay them out. A flowering plant whose taxa do not say is drawn with single flowers.

appearance.organs.flower.shape.template.why: Single flowers are drawn on a flower card, heads of florets on a head card and spikelets on a spikelet card; the inflorescence rules lay them out. A flowering plant whose taxa do not say is drawn with single flowers.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.involu.why: A cluster's bracts at its foot that are no spathe stand in a ring round the axis below its lowest flower, as many as its flora counts: an umbel's involucre, a four o'clock's calyx-like cup of five, the leafy bracts ringing a purslane's flowers.
Each bract of an involucre is as long, for the cluster, as its flora measures it.
A cluster's bracts are drawn as its flora names them: green and leafy, showy like petals in the flowers' colour, or small dry scales.

appearance.organs.*.inflorescence.floral.why: Where its flora gives a bract under each flower, each flower of a cluster stands over one where its stalk leaves the axis, as long for the cluster as the flora measures them: a saltcedar's raceme's narrow scales, about as long as its tiny flowers.

appearance.organs.*.season.why: A plant whose flowering and fruiting months are stated flowers and fruits in them: each flowering look its files leave without a year is a bud, a flower and fruit on the days its months give, and gone outside them. A flower's look becomes its look in flower and its own look its fruit, which the fruit's rules draw; a head or a spikelet is drawn as itself in each stage.

appearance.organs.*.season.bud.why: A look's buds show half a month before the first month it flowers in; for one that flowers from January, in the December before, its whole year counted from then. A plant that flowers all year draws its organs in cohorts a quarter of the year apart (its season's stagger), each budding from New Year's Day of its own year.

appearance.organs.*.season.flower.why: Its first flowers open as the first month it flowers in begins; a cohort of a plant that flowers all year opens a fortnight after its buds show.

appearance.organs.*.season.fruit.rule: max(flowering_months) - min(flowering_months) >= 11 ? 135 : max(month_start(min(flowering_months)) + 1, (opening > 0 ? month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1) : min(month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1), max(month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0)), round((month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1) + month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0))) / 2)))) - opening) + (min(flowering_months) == 1 ? 365 : 0)
appearance.organs.*.season.fruit.why: Its last flowers go to fruit as the last month it flowers in ends, or where it is ripe before then, in the middle of the months it both flowers and is ripe in; a cluster's first go its units' opening days before, and a cluster that opens on as its first fruit ripen keeps flowering to the end of its months. A cohort of a plant that flowers all year flowers four months, so with four cohorts a quarter of the year apart some are always in flower.

appearance.organs.*.season.opening.why: A cluster still flowering in the months its first fruit are ripe opens its flowers one after another over those months, so it flowers to the end of its months while its first fruit ripen. A cohort's cluster of a plant that flowers all year opens over two months.

appearance.organs.*.season.ripe.rule: max(flowering_months) - min(flowering_months) >= 11 ? 165 - ripening / 2 : max(max(month_start(min(flowering_months)) + 1, (opening > 0 ? month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1) : min(month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1), max(month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0)), round((month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1) + month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0))) / 2)))) - opening), (opening > 0 ? month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0)) : max(min(month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1), max(month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0)), round((month_start(max(flowering_months) + 1) + month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0))) / 2))), month_start(min(fruiting_months) + (min(fruiting_months) < min(flowering_months) ? 12 : 0)))) - ripening / 2) + (min(flowering_months) == 1 ? 365 : 0)
appearance.organs.*.season.ripe.why: Its fruit is half ripe as the first month it is ripe in begins (one before its flowers' is in the next year), or where its last flowers are still open then, as they go to fruit; it ripens only once it is fruit. A cohort of a plant that flowers all year is ripe a month after it goes to fruit.

appearance.organs.*.season.fall.why: Its fruit falls as the last month it is ripe in ends, within a year of its buds; a cohort of a plant that flowers all year keeps its fruit until the year after its buds, as the next cohorts flower beside it.

appearance.organs.*.season.stagger.why: A plant that flowers all year (every month stated) carries buds, flowers and fruit at once: its flowering organs open in four cohorts a quarter of the year apart, each with the year its season gives; one that flowers in a season opens them together.

rules.generator.params.lie_branch.note: How PlantGen draws a mat of trailing branches, a choice of the model's (2026-10-19): floras say only that lying stems branch freely (Abrams 1951 p. 412, Phlox diffusa: freely branching, the branches spreading or prostrate), so a branch at about a third of the lying nodes, to alternate sides at 55 degrees.

rules.appearance.organs.*.inflorescence..note: How PlantGen draws a flower's stalk in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): as long as floras measure the pedicel, for the cluster's length.

rules.appearance.organs.flower.infloresc.note: How PlantGen draws a flower borne in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): the flowering organ is the cluster, as long as floras measure the inflorescence, its flowers as wide as they measure the flower, laid out by the cluster kind the taxa state.

rules.appearance.organs.bloom.infloresce.note: How PlantGen draws a flower borne in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): the flowering organ is the cluster, as long as floras measure the inflorescence, its flowers as wide as they measure the flower, laid out by the cluster kind the taxa state.

rules.appearance.organs.*.inflorescence..note: How PlantGen draws a flower borne in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): the flowering organ is the cluster, as long as floras measure the inflorescence, its flowers as wide as they measure the flower, laid out by the cluster kind the taxa state.

rules.generator.params.bud_size.note: How PlantGen sizes a bud (morphology terms to drawing rules, 2026-10-19): a herb's bud card, its largest bud, is as long as the stated bud (bud_length_m), where before every herb without a hand value drew the forb's 12 mm (Flora of China vol. 7 (2008), Papaver somniferum: flower buds 1.5-3.5 x 1-3 cm).

rules.generator.params.nod.note: How PlantGen draws a bud's posture (morphology terms to drawing rules, 2026-10-19): a nodding bud (Flora of China vol. 7 (2008), Papaver somniferum: flower buds nutant at first, erect at anthesis) faces nearly straight down, its stalk bent over 160 degrees, as poppy buds hang in photographs.

rules.generator.params.hook.note: How PlantGen draws a bud's posture (morphology terms to drawing rules, 2026-10-19): a nodding poppy bud's peduncle is straight below and hooked in a short arc just under the bud, a few centimetres of a stalk tens of centimetres long, so the bend is set in the top quarter of the bud's stalk.

rules.generator.params.fruit_length.note: How PlantGen sizes a fruit (morphology terms to drawing rules, 2026-10-16): a herb's fruit card is as long as the stated ripe fruit at its longest (fruit_size_m), where before every herb drew the program's 6 cm.

rules.generator.params.fruit_size.note: How PlantGen sizes a fruit (morphology terms to drawing rules, 2026-10-16): a climber's, column's or epiphyte's fruit is as long as the stated ripe fruit at its longest (fruit_size_m).

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.kind.note: Ingrouille's fruit types (pp. 162-163 of the PDF), with Simpson's Moraceae multiples: an achene, a cypsela (an achene from an inferior ovary) and a caryopsis (a grain) are small dry one-seeded fruits that do not open, a nut the same with a hard wall, so each is drawn as a plain ellipsoid; a schizocarp splits lengthwise into one-seeded mericarps, drawn ribbed lengthwise as a capsule; an aggregate fruit comes from the many free pistils of one flower and a multiple fruit from the flowers of a whole inflorescence, each a cluster of small fleshy units, drawn as drupelets.

rules.generator.params.flower_size.note: How PlantGen draws a flower borne in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): the flowering organ is the cluster, as long as floras measure the inflorescence, its flowers as wide as they measure the flower, laid out by the cluster kind the taxa state.

rules.generator.params.suckers.note: How PlantGen draws a shrub's stems from the words floras use for them (shrub habit, phase C batch 3 gaps, 2026-10-18): a few-stemmed shrub sends up 3 stems beside its first, a many-stemmed one 10, a thicket 16 over its years, from its base or its roots and rhizomes; counts chosen by the model, as floras give words, not counts. Only species that state stem_clump change.

rules.generator.params.sucker_spread.note: How PlantGen draws a shrub's stems from the words floras use for them (shrub habit, 2026-10-18): a clump's stems rise within a tenth to a fifth of its crown's radius, a thicket's over six tenths of it, as FEIS describes thickets spread by rhizomes; shares chosen by the model.

rules.generator.params.fork_height.note: How PlantGen draws a single-stemmed woody plant (shrub habit, 2026-10-18): one trunk that never forks into equal stems. Where its flora gives the height of the first fork (nightshades round 6, 2026-10-19), the stem divides there, each plant within three tenths of it (broadleaf's draw).

rules.generator.params.fork_clear.note: Wikipedia, 'Brugmansia suaveolens' (read 2026-10-19): in the initial vegetative stage the young seedling grows straight up on usually a single stalk, until it reaches its first main fork. A flora that gives a first fork's height describes a stem single up to it, so no lateral bud below the lowest a fork stands (0.7 of its height, broadleaf's draw) grows out; broadleaf revision 24.

rules.generator.params.bloom_floor.note: How PlantGen draws flowers only above the first fork (nightshades round 6, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: a fork stands at 0.7 to 1.3 of its height, so no shoot below 1.3 of it blooms; broadleaf revision 24.

rules.generator.params.bloom_hang.note: How PlantGen hangs a stalked flower (nightshades round 6, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: four fifths of the turn from its stalk toward straight down, so most hang near vertical and a few lean out, as Wikipedia ('Brugmansia suaveolens') has them hang from fully pendulous to nearly horizontal; broadleaf revision 24.

rules.generator.params.scape.note: How PlantGen draws a flowering stem without leaves, a choice of the model's: the monocots' rule (visual forms Skill 5, 2026-10-15), stated for all flowering plants (Caryophyllales families, 2026-10-19) as floras say the same of thrift's and sundews' scapes.

rules.appearance.organs.*.inflorescence..note: How PlantGen lays out a compound inflorescence's branches from the kind its taxon names them (Caryophyllales families, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: floras call Amaranthus a panicle of spikes (FNA vol. 4, Amaranthus), and without the kind a panicle's branches are racemes.

rules.generator.params.axil_racemes.note: How PlantGen draws inflorescences crowded in the leaf axils (Caryophyllales gaps, 2026-10-19), from the floras' words: Flora of China, Cannabis: female inflorescences axillary, crowded at the stem tips; FNA: pistillate pseudospikes congested. Only species that state inflorescence_spacing change.

rules.generator.params.branch_nodes.note: Five axils below a crowded branch's own inflorescence is the model's choice (Caryophyllales gaps, 2026-10-19): with the herb program's two, hemp's colas drew three spikes a branch, far apart; growers' photographs show a cola of a dozen or more pseudospikes in the top few nodes (Hesami et al. 2023). Only species that state inflorescence_spacing crowded change.

rules.generator.params.alternate_above.note: How PlantGen draws a stem whose leaves change arrangement up it (Caryophyllales gaps, 2026-10-19): floras give the change in words, not where it falls (Flora of North America, Cannabis: leaves opposite proximally, alternate distally), so the top two fifths of the leafy nodes is the model's choice. Only species that state upper_leaf_arrangement change.

rules.generator.params.lie.note: How PlantGen lays a herb's stems from the words floras use for their posture (shrub habit, 2026-10-18): a decumbent stem lies along the ground for half its leafy length, a prostrate or trailing one for three quarters of it, and the rest turns up to stand nearly upright; shares chosen by the model. Only species that state stem_posture change.

rules.generator.params.units.note: How PlantGen draws a sympodial stem (nightshades, 2026-10-17): herb revision 10's sympodium, its units counted so a plant forks about as often as the floras' figures and photographs of tomato, jimsonweed and belladonna show; the floras say the stems fork or bear leaf-opposed clusters, not how many times.

rules.generator.params.forks.note: How PlantGen draws a sympodial stem (nightshades, 2026-10-17): monochasial and dichasial are the botanist's words for one and two shoots growing on past a terminal flower.

rules.generator.params.fork_angle.note: How PlantGen draws a sympodial stem (nightshades, 2026-10-17): angles by eye from photographs of tomato and jimsonweed (iNaturalist observations 184420443, 99933529).

rules.generator.params.unit_leaves.note: How PlantGen draws a sympodial stem (nightshades, 2026-10-17): the stated count drawn as it is.

rules.generator.params.geminate.note: King's American Dispensatory (1898 text, 1905 printing read on the Internet Archive, 2026-10-17), Belladonna, p. 332, citing Kilmer: the leaves come in two sizes, the smaller about half the larger. Drawn so for every species stating geminate leaves until one states its own ratio.

rules.generator.params.flower_tilt.note: How PlantGen draws a flower's posture (nightshades, 2026-10-17): the floras' words erect, ascending, spreading, nodding and pendent as angles from straight up, by eye from photographs of jimsonweed, pepper, belladonna and angel's trumpet (iNaturalist 99933529, 88011298, 133257326, 180856408).

rules.generator.params.bloom_angle.note: How PlantGen draws a flower's posture (nightshades, 2026-10-17): the same words as angles from the shoot, a bloom past 90 degrees hanging, as the broadleaf program reads it.

rules.generator.params.bloom_stalk.note: How PlantGen stalks a woody plant's solitary flower (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): its stated pedicel length; broadleaf revision 17.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.tube_rea.note: How PlantGen draws a measured corolla tube (nightshades, 2026-10-17): its stated length over half the flower's stated width, so a trumpet is as long as the flora says, its limb as wide.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.hang.note: How PlantGen holds a fruit (nightshades round 3, 2026-10-18), a choice of the model's: the fruit's line turned toward straight down by 1 (pendent), 0.5 (deflexed) or toward straight up by 0.8 (erect).

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_cal.note: How PlantGen draws a calyx kept on the fruit (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17), a choice of the model's: persistent lobes a third of the fruit's width clasping its foot, accrescent ones 0.9 of it spreading in a star; a circumscissile one's rim a fifth of it (round 5, 2026-10-18). Where a flora measures the calyx in fruit (round 6, 2026-10-19), its length over the fruit's width.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_pri.note: How PlantGen draws a prickly kept calyx (nightshades round 6, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: three prickles down each clasping lobe's middle, as long as stated, a fifth as thick at the foot, standing out and leaning toward the fruit's tip; Flora of China (Solanum melongena) has the calyx often with ca. 3 mm prickles, Flora of British India (p. 235) the enlarged lobes often prickly. Only a clasping calyx bears them.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.kept_lob.note: A kept calyx's lobes are the flower's sepals (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17); the rim a circumscissile calyx leaves is torn into twice as many (round 5, 2026-10-18), a choice of the model's from photographs of a jimsonweed's frilled collar.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_sw.note: How PlantGen draws a calyx tube swollen at its base (nightshades round 5, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: a bulge of 0.3 of the mouth's radius, greatest a third of the way up and fading to nothing at the foot and the mouth; Wikipedia's jimsonweed calyx, swollen at the base.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_an.note: How PlantGen draws an angled calyx tube (nightshades round 5, 2026-10-18), a choice of the model's: a ridge down each sepal's midrib standing out a seventh of the radius, a groove between; Flora of China's 5-angular, Britton and Brown's prismatic.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.armed.note: How PlantGen draws an armed fruit (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17), a choice of the model's: 48 prickles a fifth of the fruit's width long, or 80 bristles an eighth of it.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.tube_col.note: How PlantGen colours a corolla tube apart from its lobes (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): the stated tube colour on the tube, the flower's colour on the lobes.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_ri.note: Angles PlantGen gives the three postures of petals or lobes (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17), a choice of the model's: erect 70°, spreading 10°, reflexed -40° from the plane square to the axis.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.sepal_ri.note: Angles PlantGen gives the three postures of sepals (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17), a choice of the model's: erect 60°, spreading 0°, reflexed -50°.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.nod.note: How PlantGen draws a nodding or pendent flower in a cluster (poppies round 2, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: the flower is turned from its pedicel toward straight down, most of the way where nodding and wholly where pendent, as fruit hang (Flora of North America vol. 3, Dicentra formosa: flowers pendent).

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.disc.note: How PlantGen draws a poppy's stigmatic disc (poppies round 2, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: a low dome a third of the capsule's width across, darker than the capsule, with one ray per carpel reaching a little past it, as Flora of North America vol. 3, Papaver, describes: stigmas 3-18[-22], radiating on sessile, more or less lobed disc.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx_sh.note: How PlantGen draws a caducous calyx (poppies, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: the sepals are drawn on the bud and fall once the flower is a tenth open, as a poppy's calyptra is pushed off by the swelling petals (Flora of North America vol. 3, Eschscholzia: sepals connate, calyptrate, deciduous as unit).

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.calyx.note: How PlantGen colours sepals and a floral tube (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): the stated calyx colour, else leaf green as before.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.sepal_le.note: How PlantGen sizes sepals against petals (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): the stated lengths' ratio.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.floral_t.note: How PlantGen draws a fuchsia's floral tube (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): its stated length over the radius the petals reach, the flower's width over its sepals' outreach.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.style_le.note: How PlantGen draws a measured style (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17): its stated length over the radius the petals reach.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.stamen_l.note: How PlantGen leans connivent anthers (nightshades round 2, 2026-10-17), a choice of the model's: a tangent of -0.1, together over the style; free ones at the usual 0.35.

rules.generator.params.bloom_size.note: How PlantGen draws a flower borne in a cluster, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 4, 2026-10-15): the flowering organ is the cluster, as long as floras measure the inflorescence, its flowers as wide as they measure the flower, laid out by the cluster kind the taxa state.

rules.appearance.organs.flower.colour.note: How PlantGen colours an organ from the colour a source states for the species, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 3, 2026-10-14): the stated colour itself, on the looks' 0 to 1 scale.

rules.appearance.organs.bloom.colour.note: How PlantGen colours an organ from the colour a source states for the species, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 3, 2026-10-14): the stated colour itself, on the looks' 0 to 1 scale.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.leafing.out.note: How PlantGen draws a deciduous woody plant's year in its leaves, a choice of the model's (leaf seasons, 2026-10-18): bare in winter, a spring flush of small pale leaves, full green in summer, turning and gone in autumn, where its leaves had stood green all year. April and October to November stand in where floras give no months, as for most temperate broadleaves of the north.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.colour.note: How PlantGen colours an organ from the colour a source states for the species, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 3, 2026-10-14): the stated colour itself, on the looks' 0 to 1 scale.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.aspect.note: How PlantGen draws a fruit from the measures a source states for the species, a choice of the model's: its width over its length, as the fruit card's aspect. Where no width is stated, the usual botanical sense of the outline words (Rosaceae, 2026-10-19): globose as wide as long, hemispheric a dome about half as tall as wide; the widths for ellipsoid, ovoid, obovoid, conic, cylindric, obconic and club-shaped are the model's choice. Every look drawn as fruit (a flower's organ in fruit too), not only an organ named fruit.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.fruitlet.note: How PlantGen draws an aggregate fruit (Rosaceae, bramble fruits, 2026-10-19): as many drupelets as the stated count, as many as the solid's detail holds, each sized to cover the fruit. FNA vol. 9 (2014), genus Rubus (eFloras, read 2026-10-19), counts drupelets per fruit from (1-)5 to 100(-150) across the genus, the main difference between brambles up close.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.loose.note: How PlantGen draws the coherence floras give an aggregate's drupelets (FNA vol. 9 Rubus, 2014: strongly, moderately or weakly coherent; eFloras, read 2026-10-19); how far apart each word sets them is the model's choice.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.hairs.note: How PlantGen draws a hairy fruit (Rosaceae, bramble fruits, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: fine pale hairs over the skin pale its colour by up to an eighth, glabrous none, puberulent 0.3 of that, pubescent 0.6, tomentose all of it.

rules.appearance.organs.*.season.note: How PlantGen draws a plant's year from the months floras give, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): its flowers show in the months it flowers in and its fruit in the months it is ripe in, as the season rules set their days, where they had shown all year and never fruited.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.accent.note: How PlantGen colours unripe fruit, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): green as the leaves are, since floras state the ripe colour and seldom the unripe one.

rules.appearance.organs.*.inflorescence..note: How PlantGen draws a corymb's outline, a choice of the model's (batch 3 review, 2026-10-18): floras word a corymb flat-topped, rounded (convex) or globose, as Dendrology (2019) p. 323 does a mophead hydrangea's; the three are drawn as tips level, on a half sphere and round a ball.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.infloresce.note: How PlantGen draws a cluster in fruit, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): each fruit as long, for the cluster's length, as floras measure the fruit, as its flowers are drawn as wide as they measure the flower.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.shape.seed.note: How PlantGen draws the seeds of an open aggregate, a choice of the model's (magnoliid fruit, 2026-10-17): two follicles in three split, each showing its seed.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.shape.ripe.note: How PlantGen draws ripening fruit, a choice of the model's (magnolia, 2026-10-18): each fruit is ripe or not by a fixed draw against the share still unripe; the ripe ones are in the ripening colour while 60% or more are unripe, and blend smoothly to the ripe colour as the rest ripen.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.shape.thre.note: How PlantGen draws seeds on their threads, a choice of the model's (magnolia, 2026-10-18): a split follicle's seed hangs straight down from the split on a thin pale thread as long as stated, for the fruit's length; at a few millimetres it sits in the split.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.shape.cup.note: How PlantGen draws a cupule, a choice of the model's (magnoliid fruit, 2026-10-17): a shallow cup over the fruit's lowest sixth on a stalk swelling toward it, green until ripe.

rules.appearance.organs.fruit.infloresce.note: How PlantGen draws a cluster in fruit, a choice of the model's (magnoliid fruit, 2026-10-17): the units that set fruit are a fixed draw of the cluster's, and the rest are gone in fruit with their pedicels.

rules.appearance.organs.*.season.flower_.note: How PlantGen sizes a flower against its fruit, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): a stage's look is sized as a share of the organ in fruit, so a flower is the ratio of the stated flower and fruit sizes (flower_size_m, fruit_size_m), whether it is a cluster's unit or a lone flower.

rules.appearance.organs.*.season.opening.note: How PlantGen draws a cluster that flowers and fruits at once, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): where the stated fruiting months (fruiting_months) begin before the flowering months (flowering_months) end, a cluster's units open one after another from the first ripe month to the end of flowering, so the plant shows flowers and ripe fruit together as the floras describe.

rules.appearance.organs.*.season.fruit_s.note: How PlantGen sizes an organ in fruit, a choice of the model's (seasonal looks, 2026-10-16): the programs grow a lone flowering organ as wide as its flower (flower_size_m) and a cluster as long as its inflorescence (inflorescence_length_m), so in fruit the organ is scaled to the stated fruit (fruit_size_m): a lone one by the ratio of fruit to flower, a cluster only where its fruit outgrow it, to 1.3 times the fruit's length, the room an umbel's rays leave a unit on its stalk.

traits.reproduction.note: The angiosperms are the flowering plants: their ovules sit inside an ovary, and their seeds ripen in a fruit (Biology 2e, 26.3).

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.pattern.note: How PlantGen draws a divided leaf, a choice of the model's (spec rework P4): the leaf characters set a compound card's pattern, its leaflets or pinnae, the leaflets on each pinna, and whether its segments run together. A pinnate leaf's count says how it ends (odd-pinnate odd, even-pinnate even), so a flora's range is drawn as the nearest count of the right kind.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.interjec.note: How PlantGen draws an interruptedly pinnate leaf (nightshades round 6, 2026-10-19), a choice of the model's: Flora of North America (vol. 14, Solanum lycopersicum) has the tomato's 3(-5) pairs of leaflets interspersed with smaller interjected leaflets without measuring them; photographs show them a fifth to a third of the pairs beside them, so a quarter, one pair between each two pairs.

The rules also set these fields in a season's flower and bud looks that draw a flower, unless set there by hand.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_ra.note: The chart of plane shapes sets each outline word by its length-to-width ratio and where it is widest; a petal or tepal takes the same words. Its width over length (0.15 linear to 0.95 orbicular) is read off the chart's classes, the model's choice within them.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.flare.note: The usual botanical sense of the solid-shape words floras use for fruit: ovoid widest below the middle, obovoid above it, obconic a cone with its point at the base, club-shaped swelling from a long narrow base, globose and ellipsoid symmetric. How far each widens is the model's choice.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.taper.note: The chart of plane shapes: ovate and lanceolate outlines are widest below the middle and narrow to the tip, obovate and spatulate ones widest above it and full to the tip, elliptic and oblong ones symmetric. Drawn as the flower card's taper powers (0.45 round to 1.3 straight to a point), the model's choice.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.point.note: Simpson (Plant Systematics, pp. 526-527 of the PDF) classes apices of any flat part by the angle where the margins meet: acuminate under 45 degrees with hollow sides, acute 45 to 90, obtuse over 90, rounded curved. Drawn on the flower card's point, 1 to 0, the model's choice.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.notch.note: Kaplan's Principles of Plant Morphology describes petal tips as entire, emarginate (notched) or bilobed. How deep the card draws the notch (0.15 and 0.45 of its notch range) is the model's choice.

generator.defaults.crown_radius.why: A crown spreads about as wide, for its height, as the built-in shrubs' median, until a flora gives its width.

generator.params.crown_radius.why: Where its flora gives a shrub's greatest width, the free space its buds fill (room_width times the crown's radius) spreads to nine tenths of half that either side of its stems, since leaves at the tips reach a little past the space the buds sense, so it grows no wider than an elephant bush 3 m across or a greasewood 1.8 m.

generator.params.fork_angle.rule: clamp(57.3 * (0.7854 * clamp(0.5 * crown_width_max_m / max(height_typical_m), 0.05, 1.5) + 0.273 * clamp(0.5 * crown_width_max_m / max(height_typical_m), 0.05, 1.5) * (1 - clamp(0.5 * crown_width_max_m / max(height_typical_m), 0.05, 1.5))), 8, 60)
generator.params.fork_angle.why: Where its flora gives a shrub's greatest width, the stems it divides into lean out from its foot only so far that, at its usual greatest height, they reach half that width either side: the angle whose tangent is half the width over the height (a greasewood 1.8 m across and 2 m tall, about 24 degrees).

generator.defaults.internode.why: A larger plant grows longer shoots: an internode a tenth of the usual height grows a shrub to about that height by its last keyframe (species-spec pilot, 2026-10-14), its crown's space still topped at the greatest.

generator.defaults.path_half.why: Shoots shorten as the wood from the base lengthens, by the built-in shrubs' median share of the crown's height.

generator.defaults.leaf_size.why: A leaf card holds one leaf and its stalk: the blade as long as the flora's leaf length, and the stalk it gives, or about a sixth more where it gives none.

generator.defaults.spur_leaf.why: A short shoot's leaves are a little smaller than a long shoot's, by the built-in shrubs' median share (32 of them, 2026-10-16), so a species' stated leaf length sizes both.

generator.defaults.leaf_years.why: An evergreen keeps each leaf two years, the built-in evergreen broadleaves' median (2 for 8 of them, 3 for 5); a deciduous plant sheds them in its first autumn.

generator.defaults.space_reach.why: A bud senses free space out to a metre, and at least twice as far as the spacing its leaves keep the shoots apart (space_kill), so a large-leaved shrub's buds still find room beyond the space their own shoots take.

generator.params.unit_nodes.rule: max(max(1, min(round(shoot_leaves / (leaves_per_node * max_shoot)), floor(4 * internode * (leaves_per_node < 2 ? 2 : 1) / leaf_size))), internode / max(1, min(round(shoot_leaves / (leaves_per_node * max_shoot)), floor(4 * internode * (leaves_per_node < 2 ? 2 : 1) / leaf_size))) > leaf_size ? min(floor(31 / max_shoot), round(internode / (0.6 * leaf_size))) : 0)
generator.params.unit_nodes.why: A woody plant's long shoot never leaves more than a leaf's length of bare wood between its leaves: where the taxon's count of leaves per shoot would spread a small-leaved plant's leaves farther apart than that (a cherry's, an aspen's), its shoots set them about three fifths of a leaf apart instead, so its twigs are leafed as densely as its leaves are small, never more than the program can lay down in one year's shoot (31 nodes).

rules.generator.params.unit_nodes.note: Corner's rules (Corner 1949; Westoby and Wright 2003): the smaller a plant's leaves, the slenderer its twigs and the closer and more numerous its leaves along them. Where the taxon's leaves per long shoot left more than a leaf's length of wood between leaves, renders of small-leaved plants showed long bare shoots (plantgen-claude project-files/woody-forms/single-leaves-2026-10-18/COMPARE.md), and open-grown photos read through measure-mask let less sky through the crown than renders (see_through 0.04 against 0.13, plantgen-claude project-files/image-data/woody-forms-2026-10-19/CROWNS.md). Three fifths of a leaf between nodes is the model's choice (branching form, 2026-10-19): with it quaking aspen, whose 4 to 5 cm leaves stood 10 cm apart, carries about 5 m2 of leaf per m2 of crown at 40 years, within the Urban Tree Database's range for Populus (usfs-urban-tree-database-2016: median 3.7, p10-p90 1.0-7.2); it also closes up the shoots of Pacific willow, vine maple, Pacific dogwood and eight shrubs (euonymus, snowberry, mock orange, red huckleberry among them).

rules.note: Sizes a shrub takes from its own facts by the built-in shrubs' medians, and its shoots' length from its usual height so it grows to it (ten Rubiaceae of the species-spec pilot, grown at 0.89 to 1.25 times the middle of their usual heights, median 1.02), as defaults that yield to a lineage program's values and any file's. A bud's reach for free space is at least twice its shoots' spacing (shrub habit, 2026-10-18): smooth sumac's 47 cm leaf cards spaced its shoots 0.74 m apart within a 1 m reach, so after its tenth year no bud found room and it stopped growing at 46 internodes; Runions et al. generator.params.pipe_exponent.why: A tree's wood keeps the area of the twigs it carries, as Leonardo's rule has it and the pipe model assumes (Shinozaki et al. 1964): a stem's radius squared is its branches' summed. At 2.3 a large crown's trunk grew as its leaf area to the 0.87, so big open crowns carried four times the leaf per basal area of measured open-grown broadleaves (USDA Urban Tree Database: 0.15-0.25 m² a cm²), and each species' ring rate made up the rest by hand.

generator.params.heartwood.why: Every twig that dies leaves its pipes in the wood it grew from, as heartwood keeps the sapwood it was (Shinozaki et al.'s disused pipes), so a trunk keeps thickening after its crown stops spreading: open-grown bigleaf maple draws 61, 85, 101 and 128 cm through at 30, 50, 75 and 120 years against the database's 50, 76, 101 and 137, where without its dead twigs it stopped at 76.

generator.params.pipe_organ.why: A leaf's pipe is its twig's: with Leonardo's rule the living twigs' pipes (pipe_tip) and the dead ones' already give measured trunks (Oregon ash 53 cm at 50 years, the database's trees 45-70 years old 68 cm), and a pipe for each leaf on top made them half again too thick.

generator.params.pipe_rings.why: No yearly ring on top of the pipes: the living and dead twigs' pipes make the trunk. The rates each species set by hand, 2e-9 to 1.5e-4, are gone.

variants.stand_spacing.why: A broadleaf tree's stand of its like is spaced as fully stocked red alder stands are: in Worthington et al.'s normal yield tables (1960, Tables 1 and 2) the square spacing of their trees per acre over the dominants' height is 0.13-0.26 across site indices 60-120 and ages 10-80, median 0.165 from 20 years on, wider than Douglas-fir's 0.115 (McArdle et al. 1961). Where the taxon's leaves per long shoot left more than a leaf's length of wood between leaves, renders of small-leaved plants showed long bare shoots (plantgen-claude project-files/woody-forms/single-leaves-2026-10-18/COMPARE.md), and open-grown photos read through measure-mask let less sky through the crown than renders (see_through 0.04 against 0.13, plantgen-claude project-files/image-data/woody-forms-2026-10-19/CROWNS.md). Three fifths of a leaf between nodes is the model's choice (branching form, 2026-10-19): with it quaking aspen, whose 4 to 5 cm leaves stood 10 cm apart, carries about 5 m2 of leaf per m2 of crown at 40 years, within the Urban Tree Database's range for Populus (usfs-urban-tree-database-2016: median 3.7, p10-p90 1.0-7.2); it also closes up the shoots of Pacific willow, vine maple, Pacific dogwood and eight shrubs (euonymus, snowberry, mock orange, red huckleberry among them).

rules.generator.params.dead_keep.note: Open-grown photos show dead limbs or twigs in the crowns of 6 of the 9 tree and shrub species tallied, the renders in none of 80 votes (imagekit runs branching-chat-woody-forms-2026-10-19, plantgen-claude project-files/image-data/woody-forms-2026-10-19/TALLY-wave1.md). A branch whose buds have all died (in shade, shade_death, or with its tips lost) stands until it falls with the dead tree's chance, snag_fall (0.15 a year, so about seven years); a self-pruning tree still sheds its shaded living limbs whole (shed_ratio). The model's choice (branching form, 2026-10-19).

generator.defaults.leaf_length.why: A stem leaf's card holds its blade and its petiole end to end, as long as floras measure them, as a rosette leaf's does; the leaf rules give the petiole its share of it. Where the herb has a basal rosette, the floras' petiole is the rosette leaves' (wild ginger, Siberian spring beauty), and its stem leaves are often sessile, so their card is the blade alone.

generator.defaults.basal_length.why: A rosette leaf's card holds its blade and its petiole, as long as floras measure them, which for a forb with a rosette they mostly measure there.

generator.defaults.basal_leaves.why: A herb with a basal rosette has leaves at the foot of each stem, as many as its taxa count in a rosette (up to the 30 a stem's foot holds), or else as many as the built-in rosette forbs mostly have (their median); one without, or whose taxa name no usual habit, has none.

generator.defaults.stems.why: A bulb or a corm is one shortened shoot, so it sends up one flowering stem (a bulb that has split into several is several plants); a rhizome or a cluster of tubers sends up a clump of them, and so does any other herb: as many as its taxa count, or else as many as the herb defaults give.

generator.defaults.adult_age.why: An annual flowers in its first year and a biennial in its second; a perennial, or a herb whose taxa name no usual life span, from the year the lineage programs on herb mostly give.

generator.defaults.maturity.why: An annual's stems reach full size within its one season; a perennial's over the years the built-in forbs' median gives.

generator.params.leaf_years.why: An evergreen herb keeps its leaves through winter into a second year, as wild ginger, rattlesnake plantain and beargrass do; its flowering stems die back unless they are woody at the base. A deciduous one loses them in its first autumn.

generator.params.stem_persists.why: A herb woody at the base (suffrutescent, a subshrub: an ice plant's trailing stems, a rougeplant's) keeps its flowering stems, which flower again the next year and stay as long as its leaves; a herbaceous one's die back after they fruit.
